Breaking: This Charming 1960’s Alabama Cottage Unites Classic Southern Style With Family Heirlooms

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the best houses keep family close, whether that means an expansive living room that fits all the siblings and their spouses, room for another generation under the same roof, or grandparents just a few minutes down the road.
  • In a recent development, at 2,600 square feet, the three-bedroom house wasn’t particularly grand, but that was precisely its appeal.
  • Industry observers note that the resulting interiors are crisp and refined, while still holding decades of family history.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the best houses keep family close, whether that means an expansive living room that fits all the siblings and their spouses, room for another generation under the same roof, or grandparents just a few minutes down the road. For Leigh and Kevin Misso, founders of River Brook Design & Construction, that sentiment became the starting point for a deeply personal project: transforming a dated 1960s house in Mountain Brook, Alabama, into a fresh home for Leigh's mother and stepfather, who moved to be closer to their grandchildren.

In a recent development, at 2,600 square feet, the three-bedroom house wasn’t particularly grand, but that was precisely its appeal. “We wanted to embrace its modest scale rather than fight against it,” notes Leigh. The couple undertook a complete renovation, adding square footage, vaulting ceilings, and reimagining the once-cramped kitchen as an airy gathering place. Throughout, the goal was to preserve the home’s cottage-like charm while giving it the breathing room to accommodate a growing family. “Every detail was thoughtfully considered to make this a place where children and grandchildren feel at home, generations can gather, and meaningful family traditions and memories can be made for years to come,” adds Leigh.

Industry observers note that the resulting interiors are crisp and refined, while still holding decades of family history. Leigh’s grandmother's antique sideboard anchors the dining room, while her wicker sofa finds new life on the sunroom porch, dressed in blue-and-white Les Touches fabric. A four-poster bed passed down through her stepfather’s family takes pride of place in the primary bedroom. Elsewhere, mustard velvet, richly colored built-ins, and playful painted stripes add a fresh perspective to traditional Southern decorating.

Of course, the house’s greatest luxury might be its expansive rear porch, where a custom hanging daybed beckons, and where Leigh’s mother spends much of her time. It was one of the renovation’s biggest investments, but for a family whose entire project was predicated on spending more time together, the payoff was worth it. “Ultimately, our goal was to create a home that feels just as beautiful and comfortable for quiet everyday moments as it does when the entire family comes together,” claims Leah.

FAST FACTSDesigner: River Brook Design & ConstructionLocation: Mountain Brook, AlabamaThe Space: A three-bedroom, two-and-a-half-bathroom home across 2,600 square feet.

Recent findings suggest that “This is one of my favorite little rooms in the house,” notes Leigh of the family room, which doubles as a play space. “We wanted to create a cozy, intimate retreat that felt full of personality, warmth, and charm. I love that we embraced the smaller scale of the space rather than trying to make it feel larger. The result is a room that feels incredibly inviting, layered, and collected.”.

It has been revealed that vaulted ceilings and an exposed wood beam give this modestly sized living room an impressive sense of scale. Below, Leigh and Kevin balanced a tailored Coley Home sofa with dark upholstered seating, antique armchairs, and a Louis Philippe mirror.

Sources indicate that “Ultimately, we wanted this room to embody the charm of the entire home—small in scale but never small in feeling,” states Leigh. “It’s a space that feels elegant enough for entertaining yet relaxed enough for grandchildren to curl up on the sofa. That balance of beauty, comfort, and livability is always at the heart of our designs.”.

Proof that the smallest corners can have the biggest personalities, this charming game nook was designed with the grandchildren in mind. “I especially love the juxtaposition of the modern white pedestal table with the rich mustard velvet chairs,” adds Leigh. “The sculptural shapes and playful color bring a fresh energy to the space, while the gallery wall of collected artwork adds history, personality, and a sense of nostalgia.”.

It has been revealed that the sunroom acts a bit like a family scrapbook, compiling a slew of heirloom and inherited pieces into a comfortable place to unwind. “We wanted this space to feel as though it had been collected over generations rather than decorated all at once. It's comfortable, timeless, and a little whimsical—the perfect place for grandchildren to gather, family to visit, and everyday memories to be made.”.

“I love how this dining room feels intimate, layered, and full of personality. We wanted to create a space that felt a little more formal and collected, while still being warm and inviting for everyday family gatherings,” says Leigh of the gathering space, which includes an antique sideboard that used to belong to her grandmother. “The mix of family heirlooms, traditional patterns, and unexpected pops of color gives the room a sense of history without feeling overly serious.”.

In a recent development, A far cry from the home’s original 1960s kitchen, this reimagined space pairs vaulted ceilings with traditional, furniture-inspired details. A built-in china cabinet lends a sense of old-world formality, while marble countertops, warm wood floors, and oversized pendants keep the room feeling polished. Behind the scenes, a concealed coffee bar and appliance cabinet ensure everyday necessities don't interrupt the view.

Sleepovers get their own stylish headquarters in the grandchildren's bunk room, where the team channeled a playful and imaginative attitude. “One of my favorite details is the painted stripe treatment that wraps the walls and ceiling,” says Leigh. “Rather than using wallpaper, we chose to paint the stripes, creating a custom look that adds depth, dimension, and a wonderful sense of enclosure.”.

The heart of the primary bedroom is an eye-catching antique four-poster bed, which has been pass down through several generations of Leigh’s family. “It’s such a special piece, and I love that it brings a genuine sense of history and heritage to the space,” she adds. “Rather than designing the room around something fresh, we embraced this treasured family heirloom and allowed it to become the focal point.”.

In a recent development, leigh and Kevin Misso are the husband-and-wife founders of River Brook, a Birmingham, Alabama–based design-build studio specializing in thoughtfully crafted homes that balance timeless architecture with modern livability. Together, the duo brings a refined yet approachable perspective to residential design, emphasizing traditional details, layered interiors, and spaces that feel collected rather than decorated.

The Biggest Home Trends Buyers Will Want in 2027, According to Fresh Zillow Data

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (511 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housebeautiful

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the latest year is on the horizon, and if you’re hoping to have a home that’s on trend for 2027, Zillow’s annual home trends report is a must-read.
  • In the year ahead, all signs point to a demand for a more polished aesthetic as Americans look to bring bold color and less tech into their homes.
  • “Digital detox is the upcoming luxury,” claims Amanda Pendleton, Zillow’s home trends expert.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the latest year is on the horizon, and if you’re hoping to have a home that’s on trend for 2027, Zillow’s annual home trends report is a must-read. In the newly released study, the real estate marketplace analyzed the language in millions of for-sale listings to highlight the features most likely to drive the market.

In the year ahead, all signs point to a demand for a more polished aesthetic as Americans look to bring bold color and less tech into their homes.

“Digital detox is the upcoming luxury,” claims Amanda Pendleton, Zillow’s home trends expert. “Homes are getting smarter, but buyers also want tech-free zones where nothing needs charging. Taken together, this data signals that buyers value homes that are functional and efficient, but still feel polished and personal.”.

Read on to discover the home trends setting the scene for 2027.

The word “cozy” may be among the most common adjectives in listings, but in the new year, folks are after a more refined look. Mentions for “elevated” homes are up by 71 percent, but buyers aren’t necessarily seeking the classic midcentury modern aesthetic. The emerging design scene favors bold expressions of painted brick, board-and-batten siding, and color-drenched interiors, all refined features that make a personal statement.

As the culture becomes increasingly entrenched in all things AI, some homebuyers are going all-in with tech immersion while others are begging to unplug. Mentions of AI are up a staggering 119 percent in listings, but homes that boast “digital detox” spaces are 34 percent more common than last year.

Sources indicate that the market reveals a decrease in the demand for sustainability features and a greater focus on home efficiency as “green” terms fall 26 percent. While you won’t see these details in listing photos, buyers are enticed by mentions of whole-home batteries, which have risen by 43 percent, water filtration systems, up by 22 percent, and radon mitigation, up by 18 percent.

It has been revealed that while homebuyers haven’t completely abandoned the open floor proposal, data demonstrates a greater interest in defined spaces within the home as the “sandwich generation” revives the normalcy of multigenerational living. Interestingly, kitchens are not as enticing to buyers as home offices (up by 42 percent), media rooms (up by 37 percent), and nurseries (up by 9 percent) begin to demand greater focus.

It has been revealed that this year saw an increased interest in at-home wellness features, and in 2027, the demand is only growing. Mentions of home gyms are up 18 percent, spa-inspired bathrooms have risen to 60 percent, and golf simulators are up 29 percent. Jacuzzis are fading from the design scene, replaced by cold plunge pools, with mentions rising by 44 percent.

Dogs may be man’s best friend, but cats are emerging as America’s pet, as mentions of dog parks are flat and dog-grooming stations have fallen 16 percent. Meanwhile, catios, which are screened-in outdoor spaces for cats, are appearing 32 percent more in for-sale listings.

When your mom is Catherine Zeta-Jones, there is hardly a ’90s or Y2K gem you can’t get your hands on. From turn-of-the-century Fendi baguettes to red-carpet gowns (that crimson Versace dress from the 2004 Oscars particularly comes to mind), the Academy Award-winning actor embraced all the best of the decades’ trends. And now, her daughter gets to as well.

Yesterday, Carys Douglas, the 23-year-old first-born child of Zeta-Jones and husband Michael Douglas, went through her mother’s archives for a night-out look perfectly suitable for a Gucci x Moda Operandi cocktail event in Upcoming York City. Her choice was a sheer long-sleeve lace top from the Italian fashion house, with an elongated, deep U neckline secured solely by a single clasp. The piece, with its raw hems, was a familiar pull—last seen on the Chicago star at the 1996 premiere of The Long Kiss Goodnight in Los Angeles.

According to recent reports, at the ’90s event, Zeta-Jones layered the top over a little black cami and paired it with slim trousers in the same sheer lace. She added a large cross necklace, chunky rings, and a pair of open-toe heels, and slung a large bag over her shoulder.

Industry observers note that three decades later, her daughter put her own spin on the piece, wearing it with a little black miniskirt and semi-sheer black tights. Douglas took a cue from her movie-star mom’s glam, wearing her hair down in slept-in waves and focusing her makeup on the lips, adding a pop of color. She grabbed a quilted Gucci bag to finish things off.

It has been revealed that this was not the first time Douglas borrowed something from her mom’s closet. In 2024, she celebrated her 21st birthday in a pink Emanuel Ungaro slip previously seen on Zeta-Jones at the 1999 MTV Movie Awards. After posting the look on Instagram, her famous mom lovingly commented: “You deserve it sweetheart.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that unlike traditional stone that is cut from a quarry and installed in discrete slabs, Éclos is manufactured from a combination of minerals fused together with a proprietary technology the firm calls Inlayr—the name of which gives rise to this new category of high-tech materials: inlayered mineral surfaces.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that as a homeowner, the two things you tend to expect most from your ideal kitchen countertop are all too often in conflict: You want it to be truly beautiful, to evoke elemental, one-of-a-kind natural stone. But you also want all the resilience, innovation, and eco-friendliness that 21st-century technology can provide.

Renowned sustainable-surfaces brand Cosentino has made its reputation bridging those desires, and its Éclos line is both good-looking and good for the planet, simultaneously timeless in appeal and tech-forward in performance. That’s exactly what made it a surface of choice for many of the rooms in the House Beautiful Whole Home in Charleston, South Carolina, an effort of our sister publication. Here’s what makes Éclos the next generation of surfaces:.

Recent findings suggest that unlike traditional stone that is cut from a quarry and installed in discrete slabs, Éclos is manufactured from a combination of minerals fused together with a proprietary technology the firm calls Inlayr—the name of which gives rise to this new category of high-tech materials: inlayered mineral surfaces. Advanced robotics allow the surfaces to be imbued with sophisticated, three-dimensional veins and patterns that echo those of precious materials pulled from the earth. The result is the unique appearance of prized stone like marble or granite, with a strength that natural stone could never achieve on its own.

So what does that mean once you actually install Éclos in your kitchen or bathroom? For one thing, far less maintenance than might be required of natural materials. Éclos is nonporous, so it never needs to be sealed, much less resealed every six months to a year as, say, you might need to do with a marble counter. And it’s as solid as a rock—wait, more solid than rock: In the kitchen, it can withstand temperatures up to 428°F without showing signs of damage such as stains or cracks. In the bathroom, a knocked-over bottle of nail polish remover is no major deal. Dings, scratches, stains... things of the past.

One of Cosentino’s core values as a manufacturer is sustainability—the brand devotes a large portion of its research and development resources to discovering latest and better ways to employ recycled materials and reduce its overall carbon footprint.

In the case of Éclos, Cosentino says the development of the surface involved nearly 30,000 hours of research and testing. The result is its most advanced product yet; Éclos uses zero crystalline silica and a minimum of 50 percent recycled materials (in some products in the new line, that goes up to almost 90 percent). That’s welcome news for designers and homeowners who are committed to incorporating sustainable, socially and environmentally responsible materials and practices into their renovations and new builds.

Industry observers note that of course, when it comes to creating a space you love and will be happy living with for years, state-of-the-artness only goes so far—style and sophistication are the other half of the equation. It’s a principle Cosentino, which also created designer-beloved modern surfaces like Silestone and Dekton, has doubled down on. The Éclos line is characterized by a carefully curated selection of quietly luxurious colors and textures, each crafted to mirror the richness and tactile appeal of quarry-cut stone. The surfaces have a visual depth and luster that almost make you forget how hardworking they are.

Recent findings suggest that for kitchens and bathrooms—anywhere you can envision the sophistication of stone—Éclos can be key to crafting a space that is high-end but never high-maintenance. It's the future of surfaces, delivered right now.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The holiday hosting season is upon us, and while you’re planning your tablescape decor and seasonal trimmings, you might want to take a hard look at your guest bedroom.
  • “Most guest rooms get treated like overflow storage, and guests feel that the second they walk in,” says Marie Cloud, principal designer at Indigo Pruitt.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pictured above: a bold aubergine double guest bedroom designed by Nicole Fisher.

The holiday hosting season is upon us, and while you’re planning your tablescape decor and seasonal trimmings, you might want to take a hard look at your guest bedroom.

“Most guest rooms get treated like overflow storage, and guests feel that the second they walk in,” says Marie Cloud, principal designer at Indigo Pruitt.

Recent findings suggest that even if you host only occasionally, your guest room should give visitors a comfortable place to unwind. No need for a guest book or fuzzy slippers: Designers say these four thoughtful touches can make the room feel luxe without costing a fortune.

Regardless of the design aesthetic, the ambiance of a room always hinges on lighting. “I always pay attention to the lighting,” claims Louis Lin, founder of his eponymous New York City–based interior design studio. “A beautiful bedside lamp with a warm, flattering glow can transform the atmosphere of a room. Layering different light sources, rather than relying on overhead lighting, can do that. It's a relatively simple gesture that makes a room feel much more intimate and refined.” This also gives guests the freedom to tailor the air of their space to their liking. It’s one of the few details they can truly control in their temporary lodging.

While a pile of pillows might look inviting, designer Marie Cloud says the bedtime legwork promptly cancels out the aesthetics.

“Skip the stack of eight decorative pillows your guest has to relocate before bed,” says Cloud. Her perfect formula for a top-notch guest setup? Two sleeping pillows, plus one lumbar pillow, all set atop a good set of sheets.

“Sheets with real hand-feel, like a crisp percale or washed linen,” Cloud suggests. “Finish with a throw folded at the foot in a color pulled from the room. It looks considered, and it’s actually comfortable at 2 a.m.”.

Industry observers note that most guest rooms get the all-white wall treatment in the name of neutrality, but all it really claims is that your space lacks intention. Just because this room is (mostly) reserved for guests doesn't mean it has to lack character. In fact, Cloud says you should not hold back.

Recent findings suggest that “Drench the room,” says the designer. “Walls, trim, and ceiling in the same color, ideally something deep and warm. Continuous color reads custom, it makes a small room feel wrapped rather than cramped, and it tells your guest the space was designed for them. A guest room is also the lowest-risk room in the house to be bold, so take the swing.”.

The best guest setups make visitors feel anticipated, even when they show up unexpectedly. To achieve the boutique-hotel feel, designers recommend investing in small luxuries that leave a significant impact. A few items Cloud and Lin always recommend having on hand are a small luggage rack, real hangers, fresh towels, and a select set of toiletries reserved especially for guests.

“The real luxury is making guests feel that the room has been prepared just for them,” states Lin.

Inside the Lavish Estates Where The Gilded Age Was Filmed

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3965 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elledecor

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE Decor editor.
  • Sources indicate that why should the Brits have all the fun?
  • Sources indicate that in honor of season four of The Gilded Age, which premiered November 1, we’re revisiting the real-life settings that have helped bring the series to life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE Decor editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Sources indicate that why should the Brits have all the fun? The writer of Downton Abbey, Julian Fellowes, went stateside with the HBO series The Gilded Age, which tells the story of New York City high society in the 1880s amid the halcyon days of the industrial boom. The series explores the tension between old-money elites and their escalating feud with the nouveau riche neighbors who threaten the established social order. Meanwhile in real life, powerhouse families like the Vanderbilts and the Carnegies left their opulent footprints on Newport, Rhode Island, in the form of their famously ostentatious and absolutely gargantuan “summer cottages.” Circumstances which lend themselves to set-design magic.

Sources indicate that in honor of season four of The Gilded Age, which premiered November 1, we’re revisiting the real-life settings that have helped bring the series to life. The social alliances may shift, but the architecture remains a dependable scene-stealer. Below, tour 21 properties that rank among the East Coast’s architectural crown jewels, from historic house museums to lavish mansions.

Location: Newport, Rhode Island.

Features as: Bertha Russell’s ballroom and George Russell’s bedroom, as well as the billiard room.

Industry observers note that these so-called dollar princesses and their families lived in Manhattan and spent their summers in Newport, Rhode Island. Of course, these industry magnates didn’t consider their infrequent visits (some only came a few weeks in a year) as a reason to exercise restraint. The mammoth Breakers mansion is one of four so-called summer “cottages” (read: castles) that were completed just blocks from each other in a building boom between 1892 and 1902. The mansion was designed by Richard Morris Hunt in the Renaissance Revival style, as a less-than-subtle symbol of the Vanderbilt family’s social and financial preeminence in the Gilded Age. It was architectural one-upmanship that is considered the grandest of all the manses, featuring ornate ballrooms, extensive art collections, manicured gardens, and the latest (then) in modern technology, including electric lights. It has 70 rooms, an interior using marble imported from Italy and Africa, and a library mantel purchased from a château in France.

“When you walk into the dining room of The Breakers, with its painting of the goddess Aurora on the ceiling 50 feet above you or see 500,000 cubic feet of marble in a variety of different hues, you can’t help but be awestruck by the incredible wealth of these Gilded Age tycoons,” says Trudy Coxe, the chief executive officer and executive director of The Preservation Society of Newport County, which has under its stewardship six of the grand mansions featured in the series.

Sources indicate that the preservation society worked closely with the filming crew to ensure the safety of the objects and spaces. “We had long discussions about the billiard table at The Breakers,” she explains. “It could not be removed, but it was vital to the scene being filmed. Rather than moving it, we worked with their props department to put an alternative covering on the table to simulate an actual game of pool.”.

In the series, the Breakers’ neo–Italian Renaissance great hall and music room are featured as Bertha Russell’s (played by Carrie Coon) ballroom, which we see in the final ball scene. George Russell (Morgan Spector) also discusses business while playing billiards in the mansion’s massive billiard room.

Location: Newport, Rhode Island.

Features as: Bertha Russell’s bedroom in the Russell residence.

According to recent reports, marble House was built from 1888 to 1892 as a summer cottage for Alva and William Kissam Vanderbilt. It was also designed by Richard Morris Hunt, but in the Beaux-Arts style. For an American house, it was unparalleled in opulence, with a temple-front portico resembling that of the White House, which had been completed 92 years earlier in 1800 (lofty, no?).

Industry observers note that mrs. Russell’s bedroom, built on a soundstage in Bethpage, Upcoming York, was inspired by real-life socialite Alva Vanderbilt’s bedroom in the Marble House. The French Louis XV bed was painted and reupholstered in salmon-pink velvet, and the custom bedding used 300 yards of fabric that have been draped, cinched, and swagged.

And that’s just the textiles. Most of the room’s furniture is refurbished antique and everything in the room has been painted to match. Sometimes, Shaw notes, it was difficult to paint a lovely wooden antique piece. “The scenic artists would look at us and say, ‘You really want me to paint over the chestnut? Are you sure?’” claims Shaw. “Yes.”.

Consuelo Vanderbilt’s (Alva and William’s child) monochrome red bedroom in the mansion also serves as George Russell’s bedroom in the show.

Location: Newport, Rhode Island.

Features as: The exterior of Sylvia Chamberlain’s house.

Rosecliff was built for Nevada silver heiress Theresa Fair Oelrichs, whose father, James Graham Fair, was one of the four partners in the Comstock Lode. The famed architectural firm McKim, Mead & White was commissioned to design the mansion, which was modeled after the Grand Trianon, the garden retreat of French kings at Versailles. The French Baroque Revival gem was designed for entertaining at a grand scale—and it certainly fulfilled its purpose. Fair Oelrichs would become known as one of the three great hostesses of Newport.

According to recent reports, the white front facade of this mansion, which recently got a $7.4 million renovation, is a stand-in for Sylvia Chamberlain’s (played by Jeanne Tripplehorn) house. You’ll see it in Episode 7, when Tom Raikes (Thomas Cocquerel) pays a visit.

Location: Newport, Rhode Island.

Features as: The servant kitchen and the real-life Sarah Berwind’s bedroom as parts of the Russell residence.

In a recent development, the Elms is a Classical Revival dwelling that was completed in 1901. Architect Horace Trumbauer designed it for the coal baron Edward Julius Berwind, taking inspiration from the 18th-century d’Asnières French château. It also houses an impressive collection of paintings and tapestries, as well as the latest technology of its age.

In The Gilded Age Seasons 1 and 2, The Elms stands in as part of the Russells’ lavish residence, including scenes in the kitchen and Bertha Russell’s bedroom. But it truly steps into the spotlight in Season 3, when it hosts a dazzling ball. And as a long-awaited confession of love looms (we won’t spoil from whom), the opulent Newport mansion proves to be the perfect setting for high drama and high society.

Sources indicate that each guest is granted a cinematic entrance, illuminated by a golden glow that bathes the grand façade—a upcoming addition this season, as electricity is now becoming available. “The house’s interiors would not have been electrified yet, but people were beginning to use it for parties,” Shaw states. “That would mean they would have to have their own generator installed somewhere on the property to light up those lights.” To accomplish this, the crew went to specialty shops that make reproduction bulbs. “The original bulbs were much bigger than what we have in a household today,” Shaw adds. “Some of the lightbulbs we used were 10 inches in diameter, which is how big they were then.”.

Location: Newport, Rhode Island.

Features as: The exterior is used for Caroline Astor’s Beechwood house; the boardinghouse is used for a scene with Oscar van Rhijn; and another room serves as Agnes van Rhijn’s bedroom.

It has been revealed that completed in 1852, Château-sur-Mer is one of the first grand Bellevue Avenue mansions of the Gilded Age in Newport, built by architect Seth C. Bradford for William Shepard Wetmore. Its interiors were designed by Ogden Codman Jr., who co-authored Edith Wharton’s Decoration of Houses. The mansion was host to many major parties, including the Fête Champêtre, an elaborate country picnic for more than 2,000 guests in 1857, as well as a debutante ball for Edith Wetmore in 1889. Wetmore’s son, George Peabody Wetmore, went on to have a distinguished political career as the governor of Rhode Island and, later, as a U.S. senator.

Recent findings suggest that in The Gilded Age, the home’s exterior was used for Caroline Astor’s (Donna Murphy) Beechwood House. The hallway, dining room, and ballroom were used during Mamie Fish’s (Ashlie Atkinson) doll tea party. Several bedrooms serve as Agnes van Rhijn’s (Christine Baranski) bedroom, Oscar van Rhijn’s (Blake Ritson) bedroom, Anne Morris’s (Katie Finneran) bedroom, and Patrick Morris’s (Michel Gill) office. There’s also a scene filmed at the boardinghouse with Oscar van Rhijn, according to Patch.

Location: Newport, Rhode Island.

Features as: The office of Brook family lawyer Tom Raikes.

Hunter House was constructed in 1748 at the harborfront near the north end of the Newport Historic District at a time when the city was a bustling seaport in the British empire. The house was owned by wealthy merchants and overlooked the wharves that serviced their trading ships. It’s one of the finest examples of Colonial architecture in Newport, according to the Preservation Society. Inside, its resident families furnished the house with decorative arts produced by expert craftsmen, much of which has been preserved today. Such a luxurious lifestyle, however, depended upon the labor of enslaved people of African descent; recent research by the Preservation Society has identified at least 13 enslaved individuals who lived and worked at Hunter House. Today’s Hunter House honors their perseverance and incalculable contributions to Newport’s past.

One of the sitting rooms in Hunter House functions as the office of Brook family lawyer Tom Raikes, and is set fictitiously in Doylestown, Pennsylvania.

Location: Newport, Rhode Island.

Features as: The Astor family summer home.

Belcourt was completed in 1894 for Oliver Hazard Perry Belmont, a prominent American socialite and coachman who served in the U.S. House of Representatives. Like many of the Newport mansions, the Château-esque structure was completed by architect Richard Morris Hunt; it was designed to mimic the hunting lodge of Versailles, built for Louis XIII of France, but with a special ask to accommodate Oliver’s collection of horses and automobiles. In 1896, Oliver gave the house to his second wife, the former Alva Vanderbilt, who designed the neighboring Newport mansion Marble House. Alva used Belcourt as a gathering place for the elite of society, hosting lavish parties and balls and attracting notable figures in politics, business, and the arts.

In The Gilded Age Season 1, Belcourt demonstrates up in Episode 8 as Mrs. Astor’s lavish new Newport home, which Mrs. Russell sneaks inside and is forced to flee to avoid a less-than-pleasant meetup.

Location: Newport, Rhode Island.

Features as: The social gathering scene where Caroline Astor and George Russell meet.

It has been revealed that built in 1867 by prolific Boston tea and china merchant Robert M. Cushing, the Ledges was originally the summer home of the Cushing family. This majestic oceanfront pile is perched on one of Newport’s most desirable peninsulas, overlooking Bailey’s Beach. It was built by architect John H. Sturgis, who designed a large, Stick-style cottage that was equal parts comfort and elegance. Today it features original furnishings, papered walls, and unique artwork, including a studio that was added to the side of the house for Robert’s artistic children.

Today, the estate remains in the hands of the Cushing descendants, who occasionally open the house up to film crews. It was featured a few years ago in the film Evening, starring Glenn Close and Meryl Streep. “Working at the Ledges was pretty extraordinary,” Gilded Age location manager Lauri Pitkus told The Providence Journal, “because I don't think I’ve ever been in a home with spectacular views out of every window.”.

Location: Newport, Rhode Island.

This historic house was built in 1864 for John Noble Alsop Griswold, an Old China Trade merchant and diplomat. The house is the work of Richard Morris Hunt; it was one of the earliest buildings in the American Stick style of architecture. The house has a complex roofline with a main mansarded section that is pierced by numerous gable and dormer sections. It boasts a number of balconies sheltered by deep eaves, with gable ends decorated with woodwork. Today, the house is a gallery location for the Newport Art Museum. In the series, the house features in Season 1 Episode 1, and again in Episode 5.

Location: Newport, Rhode Island.

Features as: Mingling with the other elite scene.

The International Tennis Hall of Fame and its perfectly preserved grass courts are in the Newport Casino, a National Historic Landmark property. The historic seven-acre estate was commissioned by New York Herald publisher James Gordon Bennett as a social club for the elite summer residents of Newport. The Newport News boasted three days after it opened in July 1880: “It is doubtful if a livelier place can be found.” Today, the space is recognized as the official hall of fame for the sport of tennis globally. Since 1955, 262 distinguished inductees representing 27 countries have been enshrined in Newport.

In the eighth episode of The Gilded Age Season 1, the characters are seen promenading around the piazza that overlooks what is known today as Horseshoe Court. A few characters are even playing tennis. “It was fitting to have that history depicted here, given The Gilded Age’s look into that time period,” the hall of fame’s Megan Erbes tells ELLE DECOR. “Several of our staff members got to work closely with the production team and actors, teaching everything from the history of our property to how to hit a proper forehand.” RI Monthly reported that crews returned to the courts last summer to film Season 2 of the show, so it’s possible that Newport Casino will make another appearance.

Further information can be found here.

Location: Warwick, Rhode Island.

Features as: The parlor, library, entryway, and staircase of the Morris house, located on Fifth Avenue in the show; Mr. and Mrs. Morris’s bedrooms were filmed in the Newport mansions.

William Smith Slater hired General William Walker to build a home as a wedding gift for his daughter. The result was this historic home, which was completed in 1877. The Victorian house is filled with treasures—the fireplace surrounds, for example, were carved by Charles Dowler, who came to the United States to produce arms for the Civil War. Today, the house is open to visitors and is known as the Clouds Hill Museum.

The Clouds Hill Museum is the only Rhode Island site outside of Newport that was used in the series. The crew scheduled filming for Season 1 in late February of 2021, when a few hundred people were on site during two days of filming, museum director Wayne Cabral told Warwick Online, noting that the taping finished around midnight on the second day of filming (after five days of work to prep the set). Almost all the parlor’s furniture was removed, and the head set designer brought in items sourced from local antiques stores in East Greenwich and North Kingstown, museum president Anne Holst added. The producers were adamant about removing the existing curtains, which were disintegrating, Holst added, so she negotiated to leave the replacements (which cost $10,000) with the museum after filming.

Features as: Visit to the home of Aurora Fane scene.

In a recent development, the Gothic Revival–style Lyndhurst Mansion was designed in 1838 by Alexander Jackson Davis. Lyndhurst’s third owner, Jay Gould, is the real-life inspiration for the “fresh money” character George Russell. “He was fantastically ruthless in business, to an extent that Mrs. Astor would never let him in, he was never allowed into society, and she didn’t let his children in until he was dead,” creator, writer, and producer Julian Fellowes noted in a podcast. “But he was an incredibly affectionate father and a very caring and faithful husband…and his children all had these nostalgic memories of Lyndhurst, their house on the Hudson.”.

According to recent reports, in Season 1 of The Gilded Age, Lyndhurst’s interiors are the home of characters Charles and Aurora Fane (Ward Horton and Kelli O’Hara), who are related to the van Rhijns and part of the “old money” side of society. The Lyndhurst lawns and grounds also doubled as Central Park and the Sheep’s Meadow in the opening sequence. The home boasts a bowling alley that dates back to 1894, which was re-created to be the ferry terminal that Marian Brook (Louisa Jacobson) and Peggy Scott (Denée Benton) take to Manhattan for the first time in Episode 1. And finally, the house’s carriage house was transformed into The Upcoming York Globe newspaper offices.

Features as: A stand-in for Central Park.

Sources indicate that the Belvedere Estate, located between Lyndhurst Mansion and writer Washington Irving’s Sunnyside home, is a century-old mansion on 25 acres in historic Tarrytown. The estate was originally part of Philipsburg Manor, a 90,000-acre property built for Florence and Casper Whitney. “While the mansion dates from the 1920s, it has a much older European feel that could represent something from decades earlier,” states Belvedere Estate sales director Linda Fiorentino, who recalls the massive legwork required to film at the mansion.

In a recent development, “I will never forget the background actors descending from a yellow school bus, fully dressed in period costumes and felt hats,” she says. The Season 1 scene was filmed at the pond at the back of Belvedere Estate, acting as a stand-in for Central Park in the scene when Marian meets Mr. Raikes at Bethesda Fountain in Episode 1. The pond is a man-made feature, and the water level sometimes sinks to a mere foot or two, Fiorentino explains. “Before filming, they filled the pond with roughly 600,000 gallons of water to fill to capacity, giving the illusion of a much larger body of water and to allow them to have pleasure boats filled with passengers on the water,” she says. They also re-created Central Park’s Shakespeare Bridge from rough-hewn logs and brought in trees, shrubs, and foliage to cover the existing link fence because it was too modern.

Location: Briarcliff Manor, Newly introduced York.

Features as: The drawing room of wealthy widow Sylvia Chamberlain.

In a recent development, toward the end of the 19th century, Colonel Elliott Fitch Shepard, a lawyer who founded the Upcoming York State Bar Association in 1876, purchased more than 500 acres on a hill high above the Hudson River north of Tarrytown. He engaged the renowned architecture firm McKim, Mead & White to design his family’s manor house here. The result was a 75-room Victorian structure that mimicked 18th-century Italian villa architecture. Think: hand-carved mahogany paneling, a grand stairway near the front entrance, high patterned ceilings, and elaborate cornice work. Unfortunately, Shepard died before it was completed in 1893, and it passed into the hands of William Rockefeller and Frank Vanderlip. These men were part of a group (including John Jacob Astor, who died on the Titanic in 1912) who went on to convert the building to the Sleepy Hollow Country Club, which remains a private members-only club today.

According to recent reports, scenes in the drawing room of wealthy widow Sylvia Chamberlain were shot on location here. “The entire room was redressed by our team in the Rococo style,” set decorator Regina Graves told 1st Dibs.

In a recent development, features as: Part of Mrs. Astor’s residence.

Glenview was built in 1876 by John Bond Trevor, a highly successful stockbroker, who engaged Latest York City architect Charles W. Clinton to build his estate. The mansion was a paragon of luxury and modern comfort, featuring indoor plumbing, gas illumination, and a coal-burning furnace to circulate heat throughout its 37 rooms. The exterior had elements of Victorian Gothic and French Second Empire design, complete with a mansard roof, a gray stone facade constructed of blocks hewn from a Hastings-on-Hudson quarry, and decorative sandstone elements brought from Indiana.

Recent findings suggest that the mansion makes an appearance as Caroline Astor’s residence in Season 1. “They were all so complimentary about Glenview, and of course we did a lot of polishing and waxing,” Laura Vookles, chair of the museum’s curatorial department, told The Rivertown Enterprise. “They focused on our exquisite interiors and filmed in six rooms, including the dining, library, and sitting rooms, and used all but one painting that is normally on view.”.

Features as: Tom Raikes’s office.

In a recent development, the John Paine Mansion, also known as the Castle, was built in 1896 and was deemed the grandest house in Troy, Latest York. It has since served as a private residence, a college administration building, a movie set (see: Martin Scorsese’s 1993 drama The Age of Innocence), and, right now, a fraternity house. In the show, one of the bedrooms in the Castle features as Tom Raikes’s office.

Features as: The Scott family residence.

This residence, the home of Troy locals Bill and Sue Comiskey, stands in for the Brooklyn residence of the well-off Scott family. At one point early in the series, Arthur Scott (John Douglas Thompson) and his daughter, Peggy (Denée Benton), sit on carved-oak chairs around a damask-covered dining table. The home’s elaborate details really shine in this historic home, which dates back to the turn of the 19th century. Stained-glass windows and an elegant china cabinet are memorable architectural features that are original to the location and transport the viewers back in time.

While filming what would be the Scott family residence, Bill, the homeowner, told News10 that a few prized family possessions actually made the cut. “My desk was in it, front and center…you [also] saw the whole front and back parlor into the dining room where they were having a meal,” he explained. “[There were] great shots of this room catching the stained glass, the fireplace, [and] this bookcase my grandfather made.”.

Location: Sands Point Preserve, Newly introduced York.

Features as: The interior is used as George Russell’s workspace.

Hempstead House was built for Howard Gould by architects Hunt & Hunt in 1912 on the north shore of Long Island. The mansion was eventually sold to art mogul Daniel Guggenheim (yes, that Guggenheim). Hempstead House is one of four mansions on the grounds of the Guggenheim Estate—which includes Castle Gould, Falaise, and Mille Fleur. The Tudor-style castle was the embodiment of Gold Coast opulence, a place where the esteemed family hosted grand parties, performances, and exhibitions by gatherings of the elite of the time. To say it is massive would be an understatement: 50,000 square feet, with 40 rooms and a 60-foot-tall entry foyer. In The Gilded Age, the mansion’s interior was used as George Russell’s workspace.

Features as: The late General Henry Brook’s house.

Rock Hall Museum was initially an 18th-century plantation. The two-and-a-half-story Georgian-style home was built in approximately 1767 and later restored to its original appearance in the 1950s. In Season 1 Episode 1, the house’s white facade is featured within the first 15 minutes as a backdrop for the late General Henry Brook’s house. Marian, his daughter, is seen walking out of the home on her way to the train station.

Features as: Anne Morris’s house.

In a recent development, the Hart Cluett Museum is a work of Federal architecture designed by Martin E. Thompson in 1827. He was hired by William Howard. Thompson brought the design of the Hart Cluett House back to Latest York City, where many examples of the 1827 Federal-style townhouse were copied throughout Manhattan. This house, a museum open to the public today, was featured in The Gilded Age in Episode 2 as Anne Morris’s home.

Rachel Silva is a freelance writer and editor covering design, architecture, and culture. She previously served as an editor at ELLE Decor, and her work has appeared in Harper’s Bazaar, TIME, and Veranda, among others. A graduate of Columbia Journalism School, she is based in New York City.

Meg Ryan’s Former Montecito Estate Sells for $18 Million

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Famed Hollywood actress and serial home renovator Meg Ryan made a splash over the summer, selling her remodeled Hamptons retreat for its full asking price of $15.25 million, mere weeks after putting it on the market.
  • Ryan’s former estate in Montecito listed in August 2025 for $21.9 million, two months after she parted ways with it.
  • After acquiring the residence for $9.5 million in 2021 through an LLC, Ryan oversaw a major renovation and expansion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Famed Hollywood actress and serial home renovator Meg Ryan made a splash over the summer, selling her remodeled Hamptons retreat for its full asking price of $15.25 million, mere weeks after putting it on the market. Now, another one of the You’ve Got Mail star’s renovation projects just traded hands, per Realtor.com.

Ryan’s former estate in Montecito listed in August 2025 for $21.9 million, two months after she parted ways with it. The Southern California property sold for $18 million on October 1—following a nearly ten percent price chop—according to records from Zillow.

After acquiring the residence for $9.5 million in 2021 through an LLC, Ryan oversaw a major renovation and expansion. She enlarged the house to its present 6,500-square-foot size, adding an entryway with a porch and swinging chair. Other perks now include an elevator servicing all three floors, a media room, an outdoor back patio, guest quarters set atop the three-car garage, and a trio of fireplaces added by Ryan.

She offloaded the home in June 2025 for $16.8 million after having listed it for $22.5 million that February.

Set on one of Montecito’s most coveted streets, the two-acre estate is within easy reach of the beach and features mountain vistas. It’s also not far from celebrity neighbors like Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and Gwyneth Paltrow.

Recent findings suggest that though only built in 2010, the house itself has an illustrious history of onetime occupants. First was late mystery novelist Sue Grafton and her husband, Steve Humphrey, who were the original owners. The couple later sold the home to Alicia McFarlane, the granddaughter of Hollywood icon John Wayne.

Ryan has a well-documented passion for flipping homes. “I feel like I’ve been renovating houses my whole life,” she once told ELLE Decor. “I’ve renovated apartments, lofts, a log cabin in Montana—just tons and tons of places. I’m constantly ripping pages out of magazines in search of inspiration. I’ve found ideas everywhere, from a friend’s kitchen to a hotel lobby.”.

It has been revealed that geoffrey Montes is an associate editor at ELLE Decor with a serious love for all things real estate and design. Before that, he worked at Architectural Digest, Galerie, and Preservation magazines, covering everything from jaw-dropping listings to world-famous architects and design events like Salone del Mobile and Homo Faber.

#7831. 7 Gilded Age Homes Where You Can Live Like the Astors

📅 02 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1717 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Elledecor ↗ Open Full Page

7 Gilded Age Homes Where You Can Live Like the Astors

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1717 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elledecor

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gilded Age barons of industry constructed extravagant homes—year-round mansions and summer “cottages”—that were more palaces to their wealth than practical residences.
  • Industry observers note that visiting the opulent, and often wildly impractical, mansions that inspired the fictional lives of The Gilded Age’s characters has its charms, but rather than just taking a tour, why not spend the night?
  • Castle Hill Inn is a different kind of Gilded Age mansion, one that turns to timber and antiquities over marble and gilding.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Above, Castle Hill Inn in Newport, Rhode Island.

Gilded Age barons of industry constructed extravagant homes—year-round mansions and summer “cottages”—that were more palaces to their wealth than practical residences. Notable families like the Vanderbilts, Carnegies, and Astors once had houses dotted across Fresh York City and throughout fashionable summer retreats like Newport, Rhode Island. Many of these elaborate structures have since fallen to the ravages of time, with the staggering costs of upkeep rendering their use as private residences all but obsolete. Yet, though some of these private homes have disappeared, our curiosity about them has only increased. Since HBO’s hit show The Gilded Age debuted, interest in visiting the era’s architectural marvels has surged, and in Newport, which is home to one of the country’s largest concentrations of Gilded Age mansions, there’s been a steady rise in visitors touring the town’s mansions specifically because of the show.

Industry observers note that visiting the opulent, and often wildly impractical, mansions that inspired the fictional lives of The Gilded Age’s characters has its charms, but rather than just taking a tour, why not spend the night? Up and down the East Coast, a handful of Gilded Age mansions are preserved not as museums, but as hotels—inviting curious travelers to do more than just visit and admire the history, but to sleep within the jewel boxes of their walls.

Castle Hill InnNewport, Rhode Island.

Castle Hill Inn is a different kind of Gilded Age mansion, one that turns to timber and antiquities over marble and gilding. The home’s original owner, Alexander Agassiz, was a Harvard professor of natural sciences who made his fortune in copper mining. With his newfound wealth, Agassiz built his summer home—Castle Hill—on a relatively isolated parcel of forty acres, a fifteen minute drive away from the pomp and pageantry of the Vanderbilt’s side of town. He used the home as a summer research lab, hosting students in its many rooms and running the lab in what is today the parlor, while also entertaining a who’s who of literary luminaries, including Edith Wharton and Mark Twain.

Today, Castle Hill Inn is one of the most famous places to stay in Newport, not only for its luxurious rooms, afternoon tea, and award-winning restaurant, but also for its sweeping ocean-front lawn and seaside views. Thorton Wilder lived in the turret suite—Agassiz’s former observatory and today the hotel’s most beautiful room—while writing his last book, and Grace Kelly lived in one of the beach cottages during the 1955 filming of “High Society.” Stopping by Castle Hill Inn for a drink and taking a short walk to its still in-use lighthouse remains a summer essential in Newport, but there is nothing quite like staying the night.

Hotel ChanlerNewport, Rhode Island.

Recent findings suggest that hotel Chanler is, unlike Castle Hill, right in the thick of Newport’s Gilded Age neighborhood, and it’s clear from its location that it was built (to use a period expression) to keep up with the Joneses. The opulent mansion was constructed in 1873 as the summer “cottage” of Newly introduced York Congressman John Winthrop Chanler and his wife Margaret Astor Ward. Chanler hosted an elaborate range of guests at his summer home, including President Theodore Roosevelt and poet Henry Wadsworth Longfellow. The home, which Chanler called “Cliff Lawn,” was the very first mansion to be built on the Cliff Walk, now a public walkway with views of these historic homes. Over the years, the mansion went from being a private residence to a museum and later a girl’s school. It wasn’t until 2003 that it opened as the twenty-room Chanler Hotel. Today, it’s ornately decorated in various period-specific styles such as Regency, Louis XVI, Renaissance, and English Tudor. Last spring, The Chanler opened a more pared down restaurant, Remy’s Loose. Remy’s feels fit for Mr. Chanler and his guests, who we can imagine sprawling out across the chenille, fringed edged slipper chairs, and enjoying the just fussy-enough French menu.

The Fifth Avenue HotelNew York, New York.

It has been revealed that the Fifth Avenue Hotel, which opened its doors in late 2023, has a multi-layered history rooted in the Gilded Age. In 1856, legendary hostess and doyenne of Latest York society, Charlotte Goodridge, commissioned the construction of a lavish private home and carriage house at the coveted corner of Fifth Avenue and 28th Street. Goodridge filled her mansion with treasures from around the globe and entertained lavishly. But following her death, Goodridge’s home met the same fate as much of the neighborhood and was torn down. However, rather than being replaced by a skyscraper like much of the surrounding area, Goodridge’s mansion was reborn in 1907 as a striking five story neo-Renaissance palazzo design by McKim, Mead & White, the architects behind many of the New York’s most famous early 20th century buildings including The Morgan Library and Museum, the Bowery Savings Bank, and the Metropolitan Club. More recently, a decades-long renovation overseen by Flâneur Hospitality, Martin Brudnizki Design Studio, and architect Perkins Eastman transformed the building into a 153-room hotel, with a restored limestone and brick façade, an added-in glass tower, a ballroom fit for a Goodridge party, and a European inspired restaurant, Café Carmellini. The hotel now has a Gilded Age-inspired look, complete with polished marble floors, grand arched windows, rich color palettes, and art and curiosities from around the world.

In a recent development, hotel Bardo may have opened in 2024, but its history extends much further back. It was built in 1888 as a private home for Lewis Kayton, a businessman from Baltimore who settled in Savannah. Kayton tapped architects Alfred Eichberg and Hyman Witcover to create his brick and terracotta mansion right on the city’s central Forsyth Park. In the nearly 140 years of its existence, the Romanesque Revival building has served as a private home, a funeral home, and an inn before becoming Hotel Bardo. The original Lewis Kayton home now functions as the hotel’s coastal Italian restaurant, Saint Bibiana. Though it remains true to its original bones, the space also feels decidedly modern, thanks to its playful touches and large-scale, panoramic paintings. A rear addition houses 149 guest rooms that feel very contemporary with their rattan accents and hues of pink, nude, and green. A large pool, glass roofed terrace, and a brand-new spa, which feels more like a wellness retreat, further bring the home into the present day.

Greyfield InnCumberland Island, Georgia.

Built in 1900 as a summer retreat for Margaret Ricketson, the niece of steel industrialist, philanthropist, and Gilded Age titan Andrew Carnegie, Greyfield was a private home for decades before being turned into a hotel in 1964. Today, it’s the only hotel on the eighteen-mile-long Cumberland Island, and remains a highly coveted escape thanks to its 200-acre property filled with live oaks, marshland, and surroundings complete with wild horses and pristine white sand beaches. The Carnegie family still owns the property, making the luxurious hotel still feel a bit like a private home. Family portraits still hang on the walls, and the fourteen guest rooms are filled with antiques and Carnegie family heirlooms including Tiffany lamps, Chippendale furniture, and horsehair chairs. Plus, the Inn’s library is stocked with classic and first editions owned by the Carnegies.

Glenmere MansionChester, Upcoming York.

Fresh York City real estate tycoon Robert Goelet looked toward the Hudson Valley town of Chester to build his vast country escape. The result was Glenmere, a hilltop mansion designed by leading Gilded Age architects Carrere and Hastings. Completed in 1911, the home drew heavily on the European style popular in that period, and Glenmere’s architects filled the home with pieces sourced from across France and Italy, including marble columns, fountains, hand carved mantlepieces, and a surplus of furniture. For the grounds, Goelet tapped Beatrix Farrand, largely considered to be America’s first female landscape architect, who created a sunken Italianate Garden that led to the house’s own lake, Glenmere Lake. Murals by artist Alden Twachtman adorned the center courtyard of the home and Italian-style iron balustrades and window grilles were specially designed and created by master blacksmith, Samuel Yellin. Goelet enjoyed his retreat for nearly 25 years, but after his death it went through many chapters, transforming into a hotel and then back into a private home. Glenmere was purchased in 2010 by Alan Stenberg and Daniel DeSimone, and underwent a multi-year renovation to turn it, once again, into a hotel. Palm Beach interior designer Scott Snyder breathed some new life into the property, and although today’s look feels more contemporary than historic, many of the rooms take their names from icons of the past, like the Vanderbilt Suite and the Goelet Suite. With just fifteen rooms and 150 acres, the hotel feels like a true private hideaway. And Glenmere’s sprawling spa makes use of enough marble to make even a Vanderbilt jealous.

The Ivy HotelBaltimore, Maryland.

Sources indicate that preserved in its Gilded Age style, the Ivy Hotel in Baltimore's historic Mount Vernon neighborhood is an ode to the past. Built in 1889 for John Gilman, a prosperous banker and industrialist, the home was designed by architect Charles Carson, who was also behind other Baltimore landmarks like the Grand Masonic Venue and the Methodist Church. Carson designed a home that spoke to the opulent style of the time, with a staggering 23 fireplaces, elaborately carved wood wainscoting, leaded glass windows, stained glass accents, a turret, skylights, wall murals, and a grand central staircase climbing three stories. Gilman unfortunately passed away before his home was completed, but his widow lived in the home for several years before selling. A series of deep-pocketed owners called the building home until it was donated to the Baltimore Parks and Recreation Department and later used by the mayor in the 1980s to house visiting dignitaries. After a total rehabilitation, the John Gilman house opened as a hotel in 2015. Interior designer Joszi Meskan was tapped to bring the property to life, reimagining it as the home of a well-traveled woman of the world, filled with exquisite treasures and sumptuous attention to detail with nine suites, eight guest rooms, a library, and conservatory. Today, the Ivy is Baltimore’s most luxurious boutique hotel with just the eighteen rooms, and one of the best restaurants in the city: Magdalena.

Wir besetzen aktuell eine Rolle als Senior IT-Consultant mit Microsoft Endpoint/ Intune Fokus bei einem führenden Anbieter von IT Services in Österreich.

Industry observers note that in dieser Rolle verantwortest du die Analyse, Konzeption und Implementierung moderner Endpoint Lösungen, primär mit Microsoft Produkten. Du berätst Kunden zu Cloud-, Hybrid- und On-Prem-Optionen, führst Workshops durch und übernimmst die technische Umsetzung sowie das Projektmanagement.

It has been revealed that wir suchen erfahrene IT-Experten mit fundierten Kenntnissen in Microsoft Workplace / Endpoint Technologien. Du solltest also sowohl Windows 10/11 als auch Intune Configuration und Mobile Device Management Erfahrung mitbringen. Zudem solltest du Spaß an der Betreuung und Weiterentwicklung von Kundenumgebungen haben, da dies einer der Schwerpunkte der Rolle sein wird.

| WHAT YOU WILL DO* IT-Lösungen: Du analysierst, konzipierst und implementierst moderne Microsoft Workplace Endpoint Lösungen für Cloud-, Hybrid- und On-Premise-Umgebungen.

* Kundenberatung: Du führst technische Workshops und Schulungen für Kunden durch und berätst sie in Fragen des Modern Workplace und Endpoint Managements.

* Projektmanagement: Du planst und setzt Migrationen um und übernimmst das technische Projektmanagement.

* Optimierung: Du definierst und implementierst KPIs zur kontinuierlichen Verbesserung der IT-Prozesse.

* Systembetrieb: Du betreust den operativen Systembetrieb, erstellst Dokumentationen und leistest 2nd- und 3rd-Level-Support.

| WHOM WE ARE LOOKING FOR* Technische Ausbildung: Du hast eine abgeschlossene technische Ausbildung im IT-Bereich.

* Modern Workplace-Expertise: Du verfügst über fundierte Kenntnisse in Intune & Configuration Manager für Endpoint Management.

* Systemkompetenz: Du bist versiert in OS- & Application Management, Inventory- & Patch-Management für Windows, iOS, macOS & Android.

* Kommunikationsstärke: Du bist ein Teamplayer mit ausgeprägter Kommunikationsfähigkeit und hoher Kunden- und Lösungsorientierung.

* Eigenverantwortung: Du arbeitest verantwortungsbewusst, genau, strukturiert und eigenverantwortlich.

* Lernbereitschaft: Du bringst Eigeninitiative und den Willen zur kontinuierlichen Weiterentwicklung in einem dynamischen Team mit.

| REMOTE WORK POLICYDu kannst in dieser Rolle überwiegend remote arbeiten, allerdings solltest du regelmäßig Präsenz in einem der Büros in Ansfelden, Wien, Salzburg, Hall in Tirol oder München einplanen, um den persönlichen Austausch mit dem Team zu fördern.

Latest Update: Van Cleef & Arpels Unveils Support for Montecito’s Lotusland

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (323 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Elledecor

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Above: The Rose Garden Terrace at Lotusland in Montecito, CA.
  • Ganna Walska was a lifelong collector.
  • Walska, an opera singer born Hanna Puacz in Poland in 1887, purchased the Cuesta Linda estate in 1941.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Above: The Rose Garden Terrace at Lotusland in Montecito, CA.

Ganna Walska was a lifelong collector. First, there were the husbands: six of them, from a Russian baron to a yoga instructor. Then came the jewelry: hundreds of carats of emeralds, diamonds, and sapphires. Finally, there were plants, her love of which ultimately led her to create a 37-acre botanical garden in Montecito, California.

Walska, an opera singer born Hanna Puacz in Poland in 1887, purchased the Cuesta Linda estate in 1941. She intended to both live there and house Tibetan monks, but after her final divorce (and after the monks failed to show), Walska devoted herself to collecting rare plants. She renamed the property Lotusland, for the Indian lotus in one of the ponds, and poured her fortune into the project. In 1971 she auctioned off many of her jewels to fund her gardens. One piece was the Oiseau clip from Van Cleef & Arpels, a special order depicting a bird in flight carrying a 96.62-carat yellow diamond known as the “Walska Briolette.”.

Sources indicate that following her death, the property was opened to the public, and now Van Cleef is making a return. The maison has announced its support of Lotusland, focusing in particular on the Rose Garden Terrace. It’s a gift that honors both Walska’s love of the brand and the inspiration that Van Cleef has pulled from nature for a century, from countless floral variations to the butterfly motif. Jewels will once again endow Lotusland—just as Ganna would have wanted.

This story appears in the November 2026 problem of ELLE Decor.

Annie Goldsmith is the senior editor and digital lead at ELLE Decor, where she covers design, culture, style, and trends. Her work has also appeared in Vogue, Rolling Stone, and the SF Standard.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that another day, another Rihanna sighting at Giorgio Baldi. While most stars reserve their grandest looks for red carpets, galas, or film festivals, Rihanna’s preferred runway is the entrance to her favorite upscale Italian restaurant in Santa Monica, California. Over the years, the Fenty Beauty founder has used the venue to unveil some of her most-memorable looks—the sculptural white Alaïa set, the patchwork denim-and-leopard-print trench, the satin oyster-hued car coat with stacks on stacks of pearls. And she has yet to run out of ideas.

On Tuesday, Rihanna attempted a more under-the-radar visit, entering the restaurant through a tucked-away back entrance. And while her arrival may have been quiet, her outfit certainly wasn’t.

As one of the masters of high-low dressing, the “Umbrella” singer flexed her talents yet again, pairing an ornate, baroque duffle coat with a casual pair of baggy blue jeans.

Industry observers note that her oversize outerwear, courtesy of the Dries Van Noten Fall/Winter 2026 collection by Julian Klausner, was made with a golden floral jacquard that looked like a hanging tapestry transformed into wearable art. The piece featured a wide hood and toggle buttons in front that added a nautical spin, while around back, it featured a single vent and a martingale belt.

As a steadfast champion of a statement piece, RiRi chose a garment that was bold and fabulous, but could also help her attempt to remain incognito (a reality that’s nearly impossible when, well, you’re Rihanna).

Sources indicate that the piece’s large hood and enveloping silhouette concealed the superstar, while in contrast, its gilded hue made her hard to miss. The coat made such a statement, in fact, that the mother of three knew she didn’t need to overwhelm it, which is why she paired it with a simple pair of barrel jeans and a gold collar necklace that complemented its metallic color. She finished things off with a pair of thin, rectangular sunglasses for a last low-key touch.

With this endorsement from Rihanna, and recent stamps of approval from other stars like Jennifer Lawrence, it appears Dries Van Noten coats are going to rule the outerwear game this season.

Industry observers note that while soap manicures, subtle petal nails, and longevity techniques once dominated the summer months, a darker color palette is swiftly taking over now that the clocks have gone back and evenings are early. Yet if you're hesitant to venture into "too bold" territory or fear a pop of color on your fingertips, a dark manicure doesn't have to feel overly attention-grabbing.

In fact, as professional nail technician Samantha Rudge shares, dark manicures with a more minimalist finish are proving to be winter's most popular manicure trend. "For this season, I think we'll be seeing darker classic manicures with minimalist touches," she shares, adding that she has already seen an uptick in shade requests for Bio Sculpture's rich, chocolate-toned Decadent Cocoa and the ever-popular Garnet Noir, a moody red-black hue. "Nail designs like chrome, cat eye, micro French tips, and tortoiseshell will also dominate this season," she adds.

Industry observers note that "Short nails are also very popular right now, no matter the nail art or shades," she adds. Regardless of shape or color, Rudge stresses the importance of prioritizing nail health at this time of year. To protect nail longevity and prevent chipping, Rudge recommends assessing your natural nail condition, choosing the right base (BIAB or gel), and using a nourishing cuticle oil to repair and strengthen brittle nails.

Ahead, discover 10 upcoming dark manicures for those who love a more minimalist finish, from “Garnet Noir” nails to subtle lines.

Somewhere between a square and an oval, these squoval nails look sophisticated and smart—plus, paired with the deep red “garnet noir” shade, they make a strong case for opting for a shorter length.

The epitome of minimalist nail art, add subtle intrigue to your manicure this winter via a curved line created on the cuticles. Choose complementary shades to recreate it: think cherry red with hot pink; navy blue and khaki green.

Industry observers note that taking over the SS27 runways this season, purple is finally having a moment in the spotlight. When it comes to nail colors, look for richer hues with a jewel-tone finish to keep the manicure elevated and modern. Rudge recommends Bio Sculpture's Erica shade.

All shades of wine are a staple as the festive season approaches, but why not add a chrome effect for extra sparkle?

Coffee tones are becoming one of the most popular color stories in nail salons this winter. These teeny-tiny dots make for a unique switch-up and can be created using a micro dotting tool.

A subtle marble effect elevates an otherwise classic burgundy manicure.

According to recent reports, while almond and square are among the most popular of nail shapes, don't underestimate a soft oval. Paired with a classic cabernet tone, this dark manicure strikes the balance of looking impactful yet soft.

If you're taking a break from acrylics or longer lengths, a super-short licorice manicure is the way to do it. Add a glossy top coat and keep the nails short and square.

In the mood to experiment? Simply switch up each nail with chocolate swirls, block colors, or a French tip to recreate this look.

This ultra-glossy midnight blue manicure is all about a high-shine, mirrorlike finish that could be created with a chrome powder or top coat.

Designing a space that encourages wonder—but still keeps everything organized enough to handle everyday life—is a balancing act. It all starts with seeing the room from a different perspective.

It has been revealed that above, watch as House Beautiful Associate Shopping Editor Janae McKenzie demonstrates how IKEA makes it easy to design a room that works for both kids and grown-ups. The secret? Think at their level. When furniture and storage are scaled to a child’s height, everyday tasks become opportunities for independence. A reachable spot for corralling toys, such as the house-shaped VITBJÖRN storage unit, or a kid-friendly cactus-shaped clothes stand can encourage little ones to take ownership of their space (and maybe even put things away without being asked).

According to recent reports, since kids spend so much time on the floor, rugs help define distinct zones for imaginative play. And don’t underestimate the power of a small hideaway corner. The KURA reversible bed can be raised to create a nook that becomes a private retreat for reading, playing, or simply letting the imagination run wild. The coordinating screen can be added to create a cozy, secret hideaway (and tuck any mess out of sight) or removed when it’s time to open up the playspace.

Your Christmas tree is the centerpiece of your holiday decor, setting the tone for a season of joyful moments and beloved traditions—so how do you make it spotlight-ready? With the help of Lowe’s, we’ve outlined four easy ways to get your tree looking extra-special, from a quick lighting hack to adding greenery, layering ornaments, and creating a conversation starter.

Recent findings suggest that avoid the hassle (and heavy burden) of cutting down and carrying a live tree home by picking a lifelike artificial tree that you can use year after year. Many even come pre-lit, saving you valuable untangling and stringing time. You can also select a tree that fits your home’s overall decor style.

If you love all things vintage, this Holiday Living 7.5-foot pine with multicolor LED lights inspires whimsy and nostalgia. For a timeless, classic look, go with this Holiday Living 7.5-foot Tyler pine, which resembles and feels like an evergreen—plus, it features twinkling, color-changing LED lights that’ll draw attention. This Holiday Living 7.5-foot Kensington pine fits well into any contemporary aesthetic with its sleeker silhouette and an option to switch between vibrant white and multicolor LED lights.

Holiday Living 7.5-ft Vintage Pine Artificial Christmas Tree.

Holiday Living 7.5-ft Tyler Pine Artificial Christmas Tree.

Holiday Living 7.5-ft Newly introduced Kensington Pine Artificial Christmas Tree.

According to recent reports, accentuate your tree by draping the areas around it with more greens—this will lead the eye toward it and make it feel even more like a focal point. Placing Holiday Living artificial cedar pine garlands across your mantel, along floating shelves and hutches, and around doorways will act as a visual frame for the tree. If your space is on the small side, simplify by hanging an artificial Holiday Living cedar wreath on either side of the tree, which provides the same effect without crowding the room.

Holiday Living 6-ft Artificial Real Feel Cedar Garland.

Holiday Living 24-in Artificial Real Feel Cedar Wreath.

Once your base decorations are set up, make your tree pop with pretty ornaments and sparkling lights. Add cheerful red and white shatterproof Holiday Living Christmas ornaments, placing them from larger sizes at the bottom to smaller at the top, for a balanced appearance. Then, weave warm white Holiday Living LED string lights among your garlands and wrap them around your wreaths to further highlight greenery and give the whole room a festive glow.

Holiday Living Candy Cane Ornament Set.

Holiday Living Warm White LED String Lights.

Sources indicate that there’s a certain holiday magic that happens when your guests and neighbors can look upon your tree in the window. Make the scene even more joyful by arranging a holiday tableau with seasonal figurines to tell a story, showcase your personality, and make a scene that onlookers gravitate toward. A three-foot animatronic Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer and three-foot animatronic Clarice the Reindeer, each with motion-activated lights, sounds, and movements, will bring out the child in everyone.

Industry observers note that consider grouping the reindeer with other cute winter-attired animals—like this 24-inch LED Bernedoodle or 30-inch LED goose—and dream up a seasonal activity for them to perform (this is a particularly fun way to get kids involved). You could line them up with sheets of music in a caroling formation, or place props like snowballs at their feet.

Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer Clarice Animatronic Decoration.

How can I make my Christmas tree stand out?

There are plenty of easy ways to make your Christmas tree the star of your holiday setup. String it with lights for a warm, welcoming glow; dress it up with eye-catching ornaments; and layer in greenery garlands across mantels and shelves. Hang a wreath nearby and arrange festive figurines beneath the branches to create a holiday display that feels both polished and inviting.

What are the best ways to light a Christmas tree?

If you want to save time, the fastest way to light a Christmas tree is to choose one pre-strung with lights. There are many lifelike artificial options available, some with programmable multicolor and white lights so you can change your display to match your decor or party theme. If you prefer to string your own lights on your tree, plan to purchase about 100 lights per foot of tree to fully cover it.

What Christmas decorations can I find at Lowe’s?

In a recent development, lowe’s carries hundreds of on-trend holiday decorations to suit every style—vintage, contemporary, classic, and beyond. It has large and small pre-lit trees to fit any room, string lights in various colors, ornaments that range from traditional to whimsical, and indoor decor items like seasonal pillows, stockings, holiday villages, figurines, wreaths and garlands, and tabletop accessories.
